name: Lawu
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Yang, Cathryn. 2012. Phonology sketch and classification of Lawu, an undocumented Ngwi language of Yunnan. Linguistic Discovery 10(2), article 410. Dartmouth College. (full HTML, journals.dartmouth.edu)
catalog_quote: Lawu's syllable template is (C)V(ŋ) with suprasegmental tone. There are 22 initial consonants, six monophthongs that may be followed by -ŋ, five diphthongs, and four tones. Like other Central Ngwi languages (Matisoff 2003), Lawu has lost Proto-Ngwi syllable-final consonants. ... 4.3 Tones This section gives an acoustic analysis of the Lawu tonal system and describes Lawu's complex tone splits and mergers. Lawu has four contrastive tones: three level pitches (high, mid, low) in modal phonation and one mid falling pitch in harsh phonation. Compared to other Central Ngwi languages, this tonal inventory is rather small: Lahu has seven (Matisoff 1982 [1973]), Lisu six (Bradley 2003), Central Lalo five (Yang 2010a).

audit.reasoning: The 'tonal' coding rests on the sole primary description of Lawu (Yang 2012, a fieldwork phonology sketch with acoustic tone analysis in a peer-reviewed journal), held in full as publisher text, with the deciding quotation confirmed verbatim at both stated locators. Glottolog 5.1 has zero grammar/phonology/sketch entries for lawu1238 beyond this article; the remaining bibliography is a comparative draft (Hsiu 2017, downloaded now, silent on stress and dependent on Yang), two Chinese gazetteer wordlists, and the ISO request. Nothing found suggests a stress or accent system; every syllable carries one of four lexical tones. no reclassification, no evidence-grade change needed.

sources.citation: Hsiu, Andrew. 2017. The Lawu languages: footprints along the Red River valley corridor. Draft, Center for Research in Computational Linguistics, Bangkok; Zenodo record 1249178 (27 pp.).
sources.quote: No statement on stress or accent anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent: zero hits). Section 2 defers to Yang (2012) for all Lawu documentation; p.2-3: the paper 'does not delve into detailed analyses of sound correspondences, tonal evolution'. All Lawu forms in Appendix 1 are cited with Chao tone numbers on every syllable (e.g. la31 ku33 si33 'stone'), consistent with syllable-tone coding.
sources.note: Only other English-language work on Lawu in Glottolog; comparative classification paper that could in principle add prosodic remarks. downloaded and read: silent on stress, defers to Yang 2012.
